newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE--Greenspan remarks spark steepening.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE--Greenspan remarks spark steepening.

text.p: Whether or not he meant for it to play out this way, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks triggred a steepening of the U.S. Treasury yield curve on Friday as the market lowered odds of a rate hike later this month.
The two-to-30-year spread widened by about five basis points to 65 on a rally primarily at the short end.

"The market took the Greenspan speech as being fairly friendly," said Mark Mahoney, Treasury strategist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "Rightly or wrongly, the market took it as there will be no tightening at the (Fed's) May meeting."

Greenspan, in remarks Thursday night in New York, said that he expects economic growth to slow later this year and into next year. However, if growth doesn't wane, the Fed "would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets," Greenspan said.

"It's not totally clear they aren't going to tighten (in May); it just seems more certain they won't," Mahoney said. "That has helped drop yields across the curve. But it doesn't get the Fed far enough out of the way to get a significant steepening."

The Fed chief also defended the March 25 rate hike, terming it an insurance policy against future inflation. And while acknowledging "scant evidence of any imminent resurgence of inflation now," he said the Fed must remain preemptive.
His comments, which sparked a big rally that started during the Tokyo session and continued through London into New York trading, were hotly debated.

Some agreed with the market's initial assessment of the speech that growth will -- and has started to -- slow. Others, though, said Greenspan's comments were nothing new and blamed the media for misconstruing the Fed chair's remarks.

"I don't think you could read anything into it that elicits an aggressive change in (Treasury) prices in either way," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "I have read all the wire and newspaper comments and the full text of his speech, and nothing suggests that he won't raise rates in May.
"The conclusion that policy is on hold is misplaced," he said. "His options are still open."
Yet short yields dropped sharply, with the two-year falling to an intraday low of 6.22 percent from 6.33 percent late Thursday, while bonds fell only to a low of 6.87 percent from 6.93 percent.

"If people make a bet (Greenspan) will not pull the trigger on a tightening, short rates will correct a bit," said John Spinello, government securities strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc. "And that's the bet being made now."
By midday, yields had crept higher, with the two-year up to 6.27 percent and the long bond at 6.92 percent.

Traders said that early last week, the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's May 20 meeting were about 90 percent, falling to about 75 percent after a market-friendly first-quarter employment cost report on April 29. The odds fell to below 50 percent on Greenspan's remarks.

The deciding factor as to market sentiment, some said, lies with next week's data, which includes April reports on producer and consumer prices, retail sales, industrial production and housing starts.

Should the bullish tone hold, Spinello said the two-to-30-year spread could widen further to as much as 70 basis points as the two-year declines to 6-1/8 percent. For much of this week, the spread hovered around 60 basis points.
He also downplayed much of the steepening, pointing instead to what he said was a better indicator in the two-to-10-year spread, which expanded by just a couple basis points.

Mahoney said there was a possibilty the two-year could fall as low as 6.0 percent if the market collectively believed the Fed was on hold for now. He noted that a federal-funds-to-two-year spread of 50 basis points was not unreasonable if the Fed remains neutral.

Friday's "trade doesn't make a hell of a lot of sense," said a head trader at a U.S. primary dealer. "To me, (Greenspan's remarks were) another warning, and the market seemed to ignore it. Or at least, he has taken the urgency out of the next tightening."
Mahoney said that "people needed to buy and used (Greenspan) as an excuse. But if it were definitive that the Fed would not be doing anything in May," he added, "we would have had a lot bigger move."
